The study does, however, show some confusion in its use of several concepts.

At one moment our civilization is called Arab; at another it is called Islamic. Ideology is sometimes separated from its class content. Conflicts between religious schools are often treated separately from class conflict. The individual is emptied of his social meaning, while collectivism is largely confined to one side alone—even though the opposing side is also collective in character and is not purely individual, as the study sometimes seems to suggest.

To conclude this critical survey of the positions taken by modern Arab researchers toward the intellectual heritage, we should finally consider the criticism that one of these researchers directs against the scientific historical method.
He claims that the method narrows the field of research for those who use it and that it offers a “one-sided interpretation of history.”
This criticism comes from Mahmoud Zayed in his introduction to the Arabic translation of Belyaev’s book on Arab-Islamic history.
The introduction says of the book’s author that he follows “the Marxist historical framework” in studying and interpreting the events of Islamic history.
According to Zayed, this framework is both a source of strength and a source of weakness.
It is a strength because it led the author to concentrate on economic questions, popular movements, and revolutions and to shed revealing light on them.
But it is also, Zayed argues, a weakness:
“He narrowed the horizons of his own research, even though those horizons are broad and many-sided. Islamic history did not arise entirely from those factors.

“It is generally accepted that any one-sided interpretation of history must be incomplete. Even if the person offering that interpretation follows a scientific method, respects the principles of historical writing, and remains faithful to them, he still finds himself forced to pour history into a mold too small to contain it.

“History, as the record of humanity, is as broad as life itself. Anyone who undertakes to write it must therefore possess a view as comprehensive as life. Otherwise he cannot avoid forcing reality and the available evidence to support one particular doctrine or one particular message, whether he intends to do so or not.

“The author of this book is at least honest with himself. He does not hide from the reader that he is committed to a Marxist interpretation. Yet the reader will find it difficult to understand the author’s aims and intentions behind a number of his terms unless he already has some knowledge of the Marxist historical framework.”
What concerns us here is not the criticism directed at the author of the book as an individual.

What is clear, however, is that the criticism begins, both in principle and in substance, from an objection to his “Marxist historical” method itself. This is the same method that we adopt and argue should be used in studying our intellectual heritage.
Answering this criticism is therefore necessary if we are to complete the discussion begun in this introduction.

We agree with the critic that “any one-sided interpretation of history must be incomplete,” and that “history, as the record of humanity, is as broad as life itself, and anyone who writes it must possess a view as comprehensive as life.”
But that is exactly why it makes no sense to say, as the critic does, that an interpretation can be one-sided while at the same time following “a scientific method.”
A scientific method is incompatible with a one-sided interpretation of history. The two contradict one another.

For this reason, the “Marxist historical” method, precisely because it is a scientific method, rejects idealist bourgeois interpretations of history. Those interpretations are among the clearest examples of one-sided approaches.
There is also something strange in the critic’s claim that the very feature that gives the “Marxist historical framework” its strength is also the source of its weakness.

If concentrating on economic questions, popular movements, and revolutions, and shedding new light on them, is what gives this framework its strength, how can the same thing also narrow the scope of research and force Islamic history into “a shirt too small for it”?
Are we supposed to understand from this that Islamic history developed apart from economic life, popular movements, and popular revolutions?

Is it really an act of forcing “reality and the evidence to support one particular doctrine or one particular message” merely to say that Islamic history was organically and objectively connected with these things?

That would mean that such a connection did not really exist, and that concentrating on it has no basis in historical reality. The only reason for doing so would then be the desire to defend “a particular doctrine or message.”
If this is what the critic means—and this does appear to be the meaning of his argument—then it is his own interpretation of “Islamic history” that becomes one-sided in the clearest possible sense.

To separate history—any history—from its economic conditions and from the popular movements and revolutions fundamentally connected with those conditions is to look at history from only one side. Worse, it is to look at it from one of its least important sides, the side with the weakest influence on the way history moves and develops.
This one-sided outlook is one of the main features of the idealist methods preferred by the bourgeoisie in the study of history.

The wording of this criticism of the “Marxist historical” method also suggests that the critic understands Marxism as explaining history through economic factors alone. This may be why he describes it as one-sided.

It may also explain his remark that “the reader will find it difficult to understand the author’s aims and intentions behind a number of his terms unless he already has some knowledge of the Marxist historical framework.”

Perhaps, then, the critic’s own incomplete understanding of this “framework” is one reason his picture of the author’s method is inaccurate. We say this, for the sake of argument, even if we temporarily set aside the critic’s ideological starting point.

In any case, it is difficult to accept such a claim from a contemporary university professor and researcher, whatever his intellectual or ideological position and whatever method he personally uses to interpret history.

The “Marxist historical” method, or historical materialism, has become one of the best-known research methods of our time. Those who use it can be found throughout the world—in universities, academies, and other scientific institutions in East and West alike, in America and Western Europe as well as Eastern Europe.

They meet and debate with supporters of other methods at international and regional conferences held continually in different parts of the world to discuss the major questions of the age: social, economic, intellectual, philosophical, and scientific.
They are also present in large numbers in the Arab world itself, including at the American University where the critic himself teaches and carries out academic research.
Nor is this true only of historical materialism as a method of research.

Marxist thought more broadly has also become one of the basic elements of contemporary world thought. Any intellectual who genuinely wishes to be considered contemporary must understand these major currents of modern thought, whatever position he may ultimately take toward one or another of them.
No one is asking the critic to adopt the method of historical materialism in his own interpretation of history. That is a matter for his own scientific judgment.

But at the very least, he should know the method accurately—its foundations as well as its terminology—so that he can criticize the method that actually exists, rather than another method created by an inaccurate picture of it.
To understand historical materialism accurately is to understand that it does not explain history through economic and social factors alone.

It takes a broad view of the many different forces that affect the course of historical development. What distinguishes it is that it regards economic and social factors as decisive, while recognizing that many other factors also exert influence and that the strength of this influence varies according to the historical character of each society and each period.
The critic is entirely free to argue against this basic principle.
What he cannot reasonably do is accuse historical materialism of a one-sidedness that is completely foreign to the method itself.
Debate over the real foundation of the theory—the claim that there is a “decisive factor” in the movement of history—is perfectly legitimate. Indeed, that question has its own history.

Throughout the history of intellectual and ideological conflict, this is one of the basic points at which two lines of thought begin to separate and eventually develop into two different ideological traditions: the materialist line and the idealist line.

As for the criticism that Mahmoud Zayed directs at Belyaev himself, there is also room to question its objectivity because it begins from a position already decided in advance against the method Belyaev uses.
This is why the critic’s view of the book conflicts with the view presented by the “publisher” on the inside front and back covers.
While Zayed accuses the author of giving a one-sided interpretation of Islamic history, the publisher says that Belyaev “offers a comprehensive study of that vast and far-reaching state...”

The writer of the introduction also criticizes Belyaev because he “believes that the Arabs, like other peoples, passed through the following stages in their history,” after which Zayed lists the stages given in the book.
But the critic never tells us exactly what is wrong with this account, or what alternative stages he thinks should replace it.
Nor does he answer another obvious question: does he believe the Arabs were an exception to the historical pattern followed by “other peoples,” or not?
“This is the historical framework to which the author committed himself in advance, and he was consequently led to force the facts and evidence to conform to it.” —Introduction, pp. 8–10
But how exactly did Belyaev force the facts and evidence into this framework?
The critic gives only a few examples that have nothing to do with the question of historical stages itself.
Still, alongside this negative attitude toward historical materialism, we should also record another, more positive side.
The professor who wrote the critical introduction and his colleague who translated the book were both willing to present an Arab readership with a study based on historical materialism.

That fact offers another sign that this method continues to break through barriers, including ideological ones. It continues to establish its broad presence in the modern age and to reach us as a method for studying our own historical and intellectual heritage—after idealist and supernatural methods have exhausted their ability to strip that heritage of its history and its connection with real life.
The earliest beginnings of Orientalism in its second form were closely connected with Orientalism in its political and military form, whose own first nucleus was the “Crusading” movement.
Contact between Arab-Islamic culture and the culture of Western Europe, however, had begun before the Crusades.

It developed through the Arab-Byzantine wars and through the long Arab presence in both al-Andalus and Sicily. In these regions, Europeans increasingly encountered Arab-Islamic culture and began absorbing its achievements. Many of those achievements—especially in philosophy and the experimental sciences—were translated into Latin and Hebrew.

European philosophical schools and intellectual movements also appeared that were influenced by Arab-Islamic philosophers such as al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, al-Ghazālī, and Ibn Rushd.
From the time of the Crusading invasions of the East, however, the Orientalist movement acquired two distinctive features.
The first was that European scholars now came into direct contact with original sources that had not previously made their way westward.
The second was that Orientalism began to develop along two lines. At times these lines ran in parallel; at other times they became closely intertwined.

The first was political and colonial. Its beginnings were tied to the Crusading invasions, which sent repeated waves of fighters and occupiers into large parts of the Arab East for almost two centuries, from 1097 to 1291.
These invasions had colonial aims, even though they were carried out under the banner of the “Cross,” which concealed their real objectives behind a religious cover.
The second line grew from the effect that Arab-Islamic philosophy, including the philosophical traditions of al-Andalus, had already had on European intellectuals, thinkers, and scientists.
That influence created a desire to discover more of the sources and achievements of Arab-Islamic culture in its different branches of knowledge.
Religious motives also found their way into both of these lines.

This helps explain why some of the earliest Orientalists known for translating large numbers of Arab-Islamic works were monks and churchmen, among them Peter the Venerable (1092–1156), Gerard of Cremona (1114–1187), Albert the Great (1193–1280), Michael Scot (d. 1235), Roger Bacon (1214–1294), and Llull (1235–1315).
The positive results of the Orientalist movement cannot—and should not—be denied.
The most important of these results are:

1 — Orientalist scholars preserved many of the original texts of our cultural heritage and helped save them from disappearance or loss during the dark centuries when that heritage was cut off from educated people in the Arab world. Those were the same centuries in which the people of these countries were themselves largely cut off from the wider course of human historical development.

During this long period of isolation, many original texts were in danger of decay and destruction. Earlier, many had also been burned, mistreated, deliberately hidden, or distorted in meaning. Whatever we may think of their motives, modern Orientalists searched for these texts in the corners of private homes, neglected libraries, and book markets across cities and capitals, and even in villages and remote places throughout the Arab world and other parts of the East. They collected whatever they could obtain, by various means.

In our view, despite the roughness that sometimes accompanied this work, it saved treasures that might otherwise have disappeared. They survived, even if outside their own homeland, and their survival was what mattered most.

2 — Orientalists also published these works using modern printing methods. Sometimes they prepared critical editions, checking both the wording of the texts and their historical background. At other times they translated them into many European languages.
This work too had serious flaws. There were many errors in understanding the texts, as well as poor choices about what to translate, whether deliberate or not.
3 — The study of the heritage by Orientalists is the issue that concerns us here.

It would be wrong to claim that their contribution in this area was as positive as it was in the two areas just mentioned. In fact, the positive side was quite limited compared with the much larger negative side.

It was no accident that Western Orientalist studies of our intellectual heritage began to become active in the second half of the nineteenth century, or that Orientalism expanded enormously during the first quarter of the twentieth:

“Some Western scholars travelled to the East, studied in its institutions, and came into direct contact with its intellectual and spiritual life. European and American capitals competed to promote Arab culture. Schools of Oriental languages and institutes for Islamic studies were established in Berlin, London, Paris, and Rome. Scholarly and historical societies were founded to study questions concerning Arab civilization. Congresses of Orientalists were held from time to time, encouraging study and providing material for research. Academic newspapers and journals devoted themselves to the East and its peoples, becoming places where opinions were exchanged and questions debated, examined, and tested.”

We repeat: it was no accident that this activity began only in the second half of the nineteenth century and then grew so rapidly in the first quarter of the twentieth, even though Orientalism itself had existed for centuries.
This development was connected to particular historical circumstances and causes.

During the second half of the nineteenth century, capitalism was approaching a new stage: the age of imperialism. It was beginning to move away from a system of open, free competition toward one dominated by concentrated monopolies. This pushed capitalism into a new form and led to a new division of the world designed to provide those monopolies with places abroad to invest finance capital, sources of raw materials, and markets in which to sell their goods.

The signs of this transformation became increasingly clear and intense during the final quarter of the nineteenth century. By the beginning of the twentieth century, the transformation had become a reality.
As part of this process, capitalist states competed ever more fiercely to seize new parts of the “backward” world and to redistribute territories that had already been taken.

Under these same conditions, and for the same reasons, the Ottoman Empire—including the Arab lands under its rule—became one of the main arenas of this growing struggle. The Arab region offered both existing and potential advantages that attracted imperialist monopolies and suited their economic and political strategies. After the First World War and the Great October Socialist Revolution, the region became even more important to their military and energy strategies.

The “Eastern Question” was one expression of this struggle. Another was the plan for the B–B–B railway—Berlin, Baghdad, Basra—which formed part of the international imperialist race to control the wealth of Mesopotamia and secure access to the Indian Ocean.

It was during this transition into the imperialist age—an age of redistributing old colonies and competing for new ones in the interests of the great monopolies—that Orientalism also began to turn in a new direction. It gave growing attention to Arab-Islamic studies, and especially to the philosophical heritage.

This activity increased further during the first quarter of the twentieth century, after the imperialist transformation had become an established reality and the Arab countries had come directly within the reach of imperialist ambitions.

The First World War gave its victors the opportunity to turn those ambitions into direct power. And the war also produced the first socialist state in history, lying along the northwestern borders of the Arab world. The Arab countries therefore acquired a new and extremely important place in the calculations of world imperialism. Their strategic importance grew still further when the sources of “black gold”—oil—began to emerge.
Some readers will ask: what does any of this have to do with Orientalist studies of our intellectual heritage, and especially our philosophical heritage?

Our answer is this: if we look at these studies apart from their historical beginnings, and strip away any connection between those beginnings and the conditions we have just described, then we are treating the issue in an abstract and ahistorical way.
An issue of this importance cannot be understood through an abstract approach, still less an ahistorical one. The same is true of other questions involving thought and culture.

The connection between the beginning of Orientalist studies of our heritage and the approach of the imperialist age needs to be explained. So does the connection between the rapid expansion of those studies and the beginning of the imperialist age itself. We need to examine these connections in their real historical setting.

We will uncover many of these dimensions later, when we look more closely at the positions taken by Orientalists in their treatment of the intellectual heritage. For now, we will try to identify the basic foundation of these relationships.

As capitalism was moving toward its new imperialist form, imperialism’s growing drive to control the Arab world required a related cultural drive as well. Political and economic control had to be accompanied by an attempt to influence Arab culture and shape its modern development.
